# Homelab VLAN Setup

## Overview

The home network is split into four zones, and the split has made it far easier to reason about what can reach what. VLAN 10 carries management, VLAN 20 carries the client devices, VLAN 30 carries the IoT hardware, and VLAN 40 carries guests. Before the split, everything shared one flat network and a cheap smart bulb could wander anywhere it liked, including towards the machines that hold my data. Now the zones are separated and the only traffic that crosses between them is traffic I have written a rule for. The work took a weekend, and half of that weekend went on getting the trunk right rather than on the zones themselves. I keep the diagram in my notes so I can redraw the whole thing from memory if the switch ever needs a firmware reset. The zones are not there because I distrust my own devices, they are there because I cannot audit every cheap gadget I bring home, and a boundary lets me stop thinking about the ones I cannot audit. The guest zone in particular earns its keep the first time someone visits and asks for the wireless password. The rules took longer to write down than to type, and that is the part I am glad I did slowly, because a rule nobody can explain is a rule that gets deleted by the next person to look at the switch, and that person is usually me six months later.

## Setup

I defined the four zones on the switch first, before I moved a single port, because a half-configured VLAN setup is the fastest way to lock myself out of the hardware. VLAN 10 holds the management interfaces, VLAN 20 the clients, VLAN 30 the IoT devices, and VLAN 40 the guests, and I assigned each zone a subnet out of my addressing plan. The trunk from the switch to the router carries all four zones tagged, an 802.1Q trunk, with the native zone kept as an unused one so a stray untagged frame lands nowhere useful. Access ports then get one zone each, depending on what is plugged in.

The firewall rules between the zones are the interesting part. The client zone may reach the management zone on the few ports I need, so I can administer hosts from a laptop. Nothing else may reach management. The IoT zone may reach the internet and nothing else, which stops a device talking sideways to a neighbour. The guest zone may reach the internet and a printer, and nothing internal at all. I wrote the rules as a short list in the documentation before I typed them, so the intent was fixed first.

DHCP is centralised, and the relay on the switch forwards requests from each zone to the one server, tagging the request with the zone it came from. That way one server hands out the right range to each zone, and I do not run four separate scope servers. Getting the relay right took two attempts, because I had the helper address pointed at the wrong interface the first time. That was a good lesson in moving one device at a time, because only one host was wrong while I fixed it. I keep each zone on its own range so the routing stays obvious, and I never reuse a range for two purposes, which is the mistake that makes a zone list impossible to read a year later.

## Troubleshooting

The problem I did not expect was mDNS. The printer and the speakers advertise themselves with multicast, and multicast does not cross the zone boundary on its own, so devices that used to appear by name suddenly stopped being visible. I fixed it by defining the specific services I actually use and letting those through, rather than opening the whole multicast range. The lesson was to move a device at a time and check what it needs, instead of moving everything and then hunting for what broke.

I also had to be careful with the management interface. The rule I keep is that the management interface never sits on the client zone. The switch and the hosts that matter are managed from the management VLAN only, and I have one port on the management zone set aside at the desk for the times I need to be in it. If I ever lose the management zone entirely, I can plug into that port and get back in. The other fault that catches people is the device that ends up in the wrong zone because a port was left untagged and fell back to the native zone. I check the port assignment before I check anything clever, since a device in the wrong zone behaves exactly like a device with a broken firewall rule. If a zone loses its gateway, the first thing I check is the trunk, because one bad trunk takes every zone down at once and looks like four separate faults.

## Notes

The split is worth it, but only because I wrote the rules down before I needed them. A VLAN setup that lives only in the switch config is one firmware upgrade away from being a mystery. I keep the zone list, the subnets, and the rule intent in the documentation repository, and I revise it whenever I move a device. I also kept the guest zone deliberately dull, because guests should not have to think about my network and I should not have to think about theirs. The next job is deciding whether the cameras deserve their own zone, and I suspect they do. The zones also made the address plan easier to keep, because each zone has its own range and a device's address tells me which zone it lives in without a lookup. If I did the weekend again I would write the rule intent down before I touched the switch at all, because I wrote half of it first and half of it from memory, and the half from memory is the half I had to revisit. The cameras will get their own zone in the end. A camera is a device I do not fully trust and cannot easily update, which is exactly the case the zones were built for, and putting it in with the clients would undo the point of the whole exercise. Until then the cameras sit in the IoT zone with the rest of the gadgets I cannot audit, and they are content there.
